How we choose what a child sees

Every concept in the app has a written record. A representation only ships when four things are true.

One: a concept, written down

Not a topic or a worksheet type — the specific understanding a child is meant to end up with, in a sentence a parent can read. If we cannot state it, we do not build it.

Two: a documented misconception

A wrong idea children actually hold, with the specific wrong answers it produces. This matters because it decides what we check: a question both a child who understands and a child who does not would get right tells us nothing, and each record lists those explicitly as insufficient.

Three: a representation named in a citable source

The picture or object a child works with is not a design preference. It is taken from published guidance or research, quoted on these pages word for word, with a link to the source. Where a source rules a representation out, we record that too.

Four: a surface that shows the problem, not the answer

The thing on screen has to be something the child acts on to find the answer — not a display of the answer with steps attached. A representation that reveals what it is meant to teach fails this test and does not ship.

What this is not

It is a method, not a result. These pages cite the reasoning behind each choice. They do not claim an effect on any child, and we have not run studies. That is set out on what we don't claim.
